commands.speak: If you watch a bacterial flask and it seems to be exploding, you have missed the peak — this equation says when it comes.
The logistic equation: the growth rate of a population is r, times N, times one minus N over K.
The first factor is how many there are — ten bacteria make new ones ten times as fast as one does.
The bracket is the brake: the fraction of the room still unused.
K is that room — a flask whose sugar can feed ninety million cells, and not one more.
Multiply the two and the population traces this S.
Early on the bracket sits at almost one, so the brake does nothing and growth is nearly exponential.
Halfway up, numbers are already large while room is still plentiful — so their product peaks right here.
Half of K is the steepest point of the whole curve: the fastest the flask will ever fill.
Past it the bracket closes toward zero and the curve flattens against a ceiling it never crosses.
Verhulst wrote this down in 1838, fitting it to the census of Belgium, and gave the curve its odd name: logistic.
It was forgotten, then rediscovered in 1920 by Pearl and Reed, fitting the growth of the United States.
Growth needs two things at once — numbers and room — so the boom lands not at the start, but at half capacity, and everything after is deceleration.
